cards.explanation: The answer is that Elijah tells Ahab there will be no dew or rain except at his word. Elijah says to Ahab, king of Israel, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (1 Kings 17:1) My big announcements are usually “the cookies are DONE,” and even those make me nervous, friends. This one is about the whole sky.

The answer is False. Elijah says, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand…” (1 Kings 17:1) He swears by the LORD, not by Baal. Ahab serves Baal, a false god (1 Kings 16:31), so Elijah is swearing by a very different name right in front of him.

The answer is ravens. The LORD says, “…I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” (1 Kings 17:4) Elijah drinks from the brook, and the birds handle the food. Birds on delivery duty, friends, and some of my packages can't manage that.

The answer is True, morning and evening. “The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening…” (1 Kings 17:6) That's two deliveries a day, and the food is bread and meat. The brook covers the drinking.

The answer is that there has been no rain in the land. The text says it plainly: “…the brook dried up because there had been no rain in the land.” (1 Kings 17:7) Elijah's own words to Ahab were about no rain (1 Kings 17:1). So the drought he announced reaches even the brook he's living by.

The answer is a widow. The LORD says, “Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” (1 Kings 17:9) The LORD is sending Elijah to Zarephath of Sidon, and a person there will do the providing. That's the LORD's plan, friends.

The answer is a little water in a cup. Elijah says, “Please bring me a little water in a cup, so that I may drink.” (1 Kings 17:10) It's a small ask, and a polite one, with that “please” right there. I think a cup of water means a lot after a dried-up brook. The bread comes a moment later as a second ask.

The answer is True. Elijah says, “Please bring me a piece of bread.” (1 Kings 17:11) She's already on her way for the water when he calls after her. I've done that to people in my bakery, and I'm still sorry about it.

The answer is flour and oil. She says she has “…only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.” (1 Kings 17:12) A HANDFUL, friends. I've dropped more than that on my apron before breakfast. And she has a son to feed too. Flour in the jar, a little oil in the jug, and that's the whole list.

The answer is True. The widow says she's gathering sticks to take home and “…prepare a meal for myself and my son, so that we may eat it and die.” (1 Kings 17:12) I think this is one of the lowest moments in her story. Elijah answers her with “Do not be afraid…” (1 Kings 17:13).

The answer is that Elijah asks her to make him a small cake of bread. He says, “…first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me.” (1 Kings 17:13) Then she makes some for herself and her son afterward. A small cake, from what she already has.

The answer is that the LORD says her flour and oil will last until He sends rain. Elijah tells her, “…for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not be exhausted and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain upon the face of the earth.’…” (1 Kings 17:14) Elijah isn't promising on his own. The promise comes from the LORD, and the end date is the rain.

The answer is False. After the widow follows Elijah's word, “…there was food every day for Elijah and the woman and her household.” (1 Kings 17:15) The jar of flour and the jug of oil don't run out (1 Kings 17:16). Elijah and her whole household eat, day after day.

The answer is that she asks if he came to remind her of her sin. She starts with “O man of God…” and then asks, “Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?” (1 Kings 17:18) I think this one hurts, friends. The text doesn't tell us why she thinks of her iniquity.

The answer is a widow who has opened her home to him. Elijah cries out, “…have You also brought tragedy on this widow who has opened her home to me, by causing her son to die?” (1 Kings 17:20) Elijah names what she did: she opened her home to him. He's speaking straight to the LORD, honest and direct. I think he's hurting right along with her.

The answer is life. Elijah stretches himself out over the boy three times and cries out, “O LORD my God, please let this boy’s life return to him!” (1 Kings 17:21) Simple words, big ask. And the boy had no breath remaining in him (1 Kings 17:17), so this is exactly what the moment needs.

The answer is True, friends. “And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived.” (1 Kings 17:22) The LORD listens, and the boy lives. That's the whole sentence, and it's enough to make me hop on my gold base.

The answer is False. The widow says, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth.” (1 Kings 17:24) Earlier she asked what Elijah had done to her (1 Kings 17:18). Now she says she knows. That's a big turn.
